Photo Analysis, #2

The Great Depression in Photos

The Photography of Dorothea Lange

The Photographer

Background
Dorothea Lange
1895 to 1965

Her photograph, Migrant Mother, became one of the most famous photos of all time.

She worked for the Resettlement Administration, a government agency, and took photos to help bring awareness of the problems faced by the rural poor and migrants.

Take your time with each photo. Click to enlarge it and look at the faces, the hands, the clothes, and the background. Then answer the review questions at the bottom of the page.

Remember this nameIn 1942 the government hired Lange again, this time to photograph Japanese American families being forced from their homes during World War II. You will see those photos next semester.

The Photographs

1932 to 1938
Click any photograph to enlarge it
In Her Own Words
“I did not ask her name or her history. She told me her age, that she was 32. She said that they had been living on frozen vegetables from the surrounding fields, and birds that the children killed. She had just sold the tires from her car to buy food. There she sat in that lean-to tent with her children huddled around her, and seemed to know that my pictures might help her, and so she helped me. There was a sort of equality about it. The pea crop at Nipomo had frozen and there was no work for anybody. But I did not approach the tents and shelters of other stranded pea pickers. It was not necessary; I knew I had recorded the essence of my assignment.”
Dorothea Lange, on making Migrant Mother
In Her Own Words
“[White Angel Breadline] is my most famed photograph. I made that on the first day I ever went out in an area where people said, ‘Oh, don’t go there.’ It was the first day that I ever made a photograph on the street.”
Dorothea Lange

Review Questions

Question 1 See photo 1

Question 3 See photo 4

Question 4 See photo 3

Question 5 See photo 5
In image #5, what do you notice about how these refugees are living?
Question 6 See photo 6

Question 7 See photo 7

Question 8
